prompt: I'm about to start working on the cDAC (the data contract reader). Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what the data contracts are and what problems they solve compared with the classic DAC and DBI; what the runtime publishes so a reader can find them; how contracts are versioned, when a change needs a new version and when an existing one may be amended, and what is fixed for a release; what the reader version is and how it differs from a contract version; and where each part is written down.
key: The entry point is docs/design/datacontracts/datacontracts_design.md, with contract-descriptor.md, data_descriptor.md, one <ContractName>.md per contract and reader-version-history.md beside it in docs/design/datacontracts/. Data contracts document a subset of the runtime's in-memory data structures — layout and semantics — as a promise that a tool reading process memory and interpreting it by the contract gets correct answers; for debuggers (live and dumps), profilers and other tools. They remove the need for DAC/DBI libraries that exactly match the runtime build, which caused security (an exact-match DAC may be untrusted), servicing (a debugger fix needs a new runtime build), acquisition and cross-architecture problems. The runtime publishes a contract descriptor: a data descriptor with global values (constants, pointers, strings) and type layouts (named fields with offsets, determinate or indeterminate sizes, not every field), optional sub-descriptors for data an external component describes, and the list of compatible contracts, each a name and a version identifier. Since #127020 (2026-04-18) versions are string identifiers (c1, c2; other platforms can use another prefix); a 'higher' identifier is only different, not newer, and identifiers must not collide on main. A runtime change not compatible with the previous contract version needs a new version; an existing version may be amended only compatibly (fix the documentation, or add optional globals/types/fields/APIs) so a tool implementing the original definition still works. The set of supported contract versions is fixed from the first release candidate through servicing; .NET 11's were frozen in #131858 (2026-08-10), which also bumped the descriptor header to version 2 so the cDAC rejects earlier development builds. Contracts refer to each other by name without version; algorithms are written as C#-like pseudocode over the Target API, and each contract file carries a generated usage table of the descriptors and globals it reads (checked by the documentation gates of #131281, 2026-07-24). The reader version (reader-version-history.md, #134072 on 2026-09-23) is advisory: the runtime publishes RecommendedReaderVersion and a reader reports IRuntimeInfo.GetCurrentReaderVersion(); a tool can suggest an update when the runtime recommends a higher one; it is independent of contract versions and does not mean an older reader cannot inspect the runtime.

sources.quote: Diagnostic data contract addressed these challenges by eliminating the need for exactly matching DAC and DBI libraries.

Contracts are described by a string version identifier. Different version identifiers represent different contract implementations. A "higher" identifier is not necessarily more recent, it just means different.

Whenever the runtime changes its implementation of data structures or algorithms in a way that is not compatible with the previous contract version then a new version of the contract needs to be defined and used instead.

When amending a contract version, the change must be compatible: a runtime that advertises it supports contract version X must be understandable by a tool that implements the original definition of X as well as any amended definition of X.
For any given major release of the runtime, the set of supported contract versions should remain fixed from the first release candidate to the final servicing build.

rubric.criterion: What data contracts are (documented layout and semantics of runtime data structures, read from process memory) and the problems they solve: no exact-match DAC/DBI, with security, servicing, acquisition and cross-architecture
What the runtime publishes: the contract descriptor with a data descriptor (globals and type layouts, sub-descriptors) and the compatible contracts with their version identifiers

Versioning: string identifiers (c1, c2), different not newer; an incompatible change needs a new version; amendments only compatible (doc fixes, optional additions); supported versions fixed from the first RC through servicing (.NET 11 frozen)
The reader version: advisory, RecommendedReaderVersion vs the reader's GetCurrentReaderVersion, independent of contract versions
